d.title: One convolution, as four facts
d.caption: A kernel slides over the input, and at each position computes a dot product with the patch under it. Two properties follow and they are the whole reason CNNs work on images: the **same** weights are used at every position (so a feature detected in one corner is detected in all of them), and each output depends only on a small neighbourhood (so the layer learns local structure rather than a global mapping).

nodes.label: Input patch
nodes.sub: k x k, at one position

nodes.label: Local connectivity
nodes.sub: each output sees k x k inputs

d.title: Every framework computes cross-correlation and calls it convolution
d.caption: True convolution flips the kernel before the dot product; cross-correlation does not. For a **learned** kernel the distinction is irrelevant — the network simply learns the flipped weights instead, and reaches the same function. It matters only when you bring a kernel in from signal processing, or compare against a textbook formula.

d.title: The output-size formula, against what Conv2d returns
d.caption: floor((in + 2p − k)/s) + 1, checked against the framework on four real configurations. The third row is the standard way modern CNNs downsample, and the fourth is ResNet's stem taking 224 to 112 in one layer. The trap is the **floor**: an input of 33 with k=3, p=1, s=2 gives 17, and the last row and column contribute to nothing at all — nothing warns you, and it surfaces later as a skip connection whose shapes differ by one.

state: the floor discards a row and column

d.title: Why the parameter count is the point
d.caption: The same transformation, 32×32×3 to 32×32×64, done two ways. A fully connected layer needs a weight for every input–output pair: **two hundred million**. A 3×3 convolution needs one kernel per output channel, reused at every position: 1,792. That ratio of about 110,000 to one is why convolution exists, and the saving is not an approximation — it is the weight-sharing assumption being true of images.

d.title: How much invariance pooling actually gives
d.caption: A 2×2 max-pool is invariant to a shift of **one pixel within its own window**, and that is all. Shift the input by three pixels and the pooled map shifts too. The invariance people attribute to pooling is mostly accumulated over many layers, and a modern network gets most of it from augmentation and from global pooling at the end rather than from the pooling layers themselves.

d.title: The shape of a CNN: spatial size falls, channels rise
d.caption: Read it bottom-up. Every stage roughly halves the height and width and doubles the channels, which keeps the activation volume approximately constant while the representation becomes less about *where* and more about *what*. The head at the top is where VGG put 89% of its parameters and where global average pooling now sits instead.

items.label: Global average pool
items.sub: H x W x C -> C; no parameters

d.title: The receptive field, and why it has to be computed
d.caption: The receptive field grows by (k−1)×(product of all previous strides) per layer — so **stride compounds multiplicatively** and is what actually buys coverage. Three 3×3 layers at stride 1 see 7 pixels; add one stride-2 layer and the next 3×3 sees 15. If a network's final receptive field is smaller than the object you are trying to detect, no amount of training will fix it.

d.title: The line of descent, and what each one changed
d.caption: Each architecture is remembered for one idea. **AlexNet** showed that depth plus GPUs plus ReLU and dropout worked at all; **VGG** showed that three stacked 3×3s beat one 7×7 for fewer parameters and more non-linearity; **ResNet's** skip connection made depth beyond about twenty layers trainable, which is the single most consequential change in the list; and everything after 2015 is efficiency — depthwise separable convolutions, squeeze-and-excitation, compound scaling, ConvNeXt.

d.title: Eighty-nine per cent of VGG16 is the part that does no vision
d.caption: Three fully connected layers on a flattened 7×7×512 map cost **124 million parameters** against 14.7 million for every convolution in the network. That is where VGG's overfitting lived and why it needed such heavy regularisation — and global average pooling (2.2) is precisely the fix, which is why no architecture after 2015 ends this way.

state: H x W x C -> C

d.title: The gradient highway, and why it is exactly a highway
d.caption: A residual block computes y = x + f(x), so the gradient of y with respect to x is **1 + f'(x)** — the one is an unconditional path from the loss to every earlier layer, unaffected by what f did. That additive one is why fifty layers train as easily as ten: the product of per-layer factors that 1.8 warned about can no longer vanish, because one of its terms is exactly 1.

nodes.label: y = x + f(x)
nodes.sub: the addition is the whole trick

nodes.label: So the product has a term of 1

d.title: The bottleneck block: three convolutions cheaper than two
d.caption: Squeeze the channels with a 1×1, do the spatial work in the narrow space, expand back with another 1×1. Compare the totals: two 3×3s on 256 channels cost 1.18 million parameters; the bottleneck doing the same channel transformation costs **70 thousand**. That is how ResNet-50 is deeper than ResNet-34 and no more expensive.

d.title: Compound scaling, and what ConvNeXt showed afterwards
d.caption: EfficientNet's finding was that scaling depth, width and resolution **together** in a fixed ratio beats scaling any one of them — because a deeper network needs more channels to use and more pixels to look at. ConvNeXt's finding was later and more awkward: most of the transformer's advantage over CNNs was training recipe and design details, not attention, and a modernised CNN recovers it.

nodes.label: ConvNeXt
nodes.sub: a modernised CNN matches a ViT

d.title: Choosing among the efficiency blocks
d.caption: Three different savings. The 1×1 changes channels at a per-pixel cost; **depthwise separable** factorises a convolution into a spatial part and a channel part for roughly a ninth of the parameters; squeeze-and-excitation adds almost nothing and reweights channels by global context. They compose, which is what MobileNet and EfficientNet do.

d.title: The transfer-learning experiment, and what it is comparing
d.caption: Four regimes on the same small dataset, differing only in **which weights move**. The result that matters is the ordering: with a few thousand images, fine-tuning a pretrained network beats training the same architecture from scratch by a margin that no amount of augmentation closes — the pretrained features are the data you do not have.

d.title: Freezing, and what it costs
d.caption: Freezing is cheap in two senses and expensive in a third. It saves the backward pass through the frozen part and lets you cache those activations once; it costs the ability to adapt the features themselves, which matters exactly when your domain is far from the pretraining data — a chest X-ray is not an ImageNet photograph.

cells.text: needs a small lr and more data

d.title: Discriminative learning rates: earlier layers move less
d.caption: Early filters are edges and colours and are already correct for almost any image task; late layers are task-specific and need to change. Giving each stage its own learning rate — typically a constant factor apart — expresses that directly, and is one `param_groups` list rather than a new idea.

d.title: Catastrophic forgetting, and why fine-tuning risks it
d.caption: Fine-tuning at a normal learning rate overwrites the pretrained weights before the new task's gradient has said anything useful — the network forgets what it knew and relearns from what is effectively a bad initialisation. A small learning rate, a warmup, and freezing early layers for the first epochs are three ways of saying the same thing: do not destroy the features while the head is still random.

nodes.label: Warm up the head first
nodes.sub: backbone frozen for an epoch or two

nodes.label: Then unfreeze at a small lr
The features survive
nodes.sub: which was the point of transferring

d.title: The normalisation trap in a frozen backbone
d.caption: `requires_grad = False` stops the **weights** changing; it does not stop batch norm updating its running mean and variance, because those are buffers rather than parameters. So a 'frozen' backbone silently drifts to your new data's statistics during training and then uses those statistics at inference — a mismatch that looks like a mysterious train/test gap. `model.eval()` on the backbone is the fix.

d.title: The standard augmentation pipeline, in order
d.caption: Order matters for two reasons. Geometric transforms come first because they are defined on the image; normalisation comes **last** because it must see the final pixel values; and the tensor conversion sits between them. Random erasing is applied after normalisation on purpose — it erases to the normalised mean, which is zero.

nodes.label: Normalize
nodes.sub: the dataset's mean and sd: last

nodes.label: RandomErasing
nodes.sub: after normalising, so it erases to 0

d.title: Augment training only, and why that is not arbitrary
d.caption: Augmentation exists to make the training distribution wider than the data. Applying it to validation makes the validation set **harder than reality**, so the number you read is not the number production will give you — and worse, it is noisy, because a different random crop each epoch means the metric moves for reasons unrelated to the model.

nodes.label: Train: augment
nodes.sub: a wider distribution than the data

d.title: Which transforms preserve your label
d.caption: This is a question about the task, not about images in general — and getting it wrong teaches the model something false. A horizontal flip is free on a cat and destroys a digit; a rotation is free on satellite imagery and wrong on a chest X-ray, where left and right are anatomy.

cells.text: when the object can be cropped out

d.title: Test-time augmentation: the one place augmenting evaluation is right
d.caption: Run each test image through several deterministic transforms and average the predictions. It reliably buys a small amount of accuracy for a multiple of the inference cost — so it is a decision about latency budget, not about modelling, and it must be applied identically to any baseline you compare against.

nodes.label: A small, reliable gain
nodes.sub: often a few tenths of a point

d.title: Why COCO's mAP is stricter than Pascal's
d.caption: Pascal VOC declares a detection correct at IoU ≥ 0.5 and averages over classes. COCO averages over **ten IoU thresholds** from 0.50 to 0.95, so a box that is roughly right scores at the loose end and nothing at the strict end — which is why the same detector's COCO mAP is far below its Pascal number, and why the two are not comparable.

state: finding it and locating it precisely

d.title: Average precision from a ranked list, step by step
d.caption: AP is not an average of precisions at fixed recalls — it is the area under the precision–recall curve traced by walking the **ranked detections**. Each true positive moves recall right and lifts precision; each false positive lowers precision without moving recall. That is why ranking quality, not just counting, is what AP measures.

items.desc: across the whole dataset, not per image

items.label: Match each to a ground-truth box by IoU

items.label: Walk the list, recomputing precision and recall
items.desc: a TP moves recall; an FP only hurts precision

items.label: Take the running maximum of precision
items.desc: the interpolation step, so the curve is monotone

items.label: Average over classes, then over IoUs

d.title: Three kinds of segmentation, and what each output looks like
d.caption: The difference is entirely in what counts as a distinct answer. Semantic segmentation labels pixels by class and cannot separate two adjacent cars; instance segmentation separates them and ignores the background; panoptic does both, which is why its evaluation needed a new metric rather than a reused one.

cells.text: a class plus an instance id

d.title: From a classifier head to a dense head
d.caption: A classifier ends by throwing position away — that is what the flatten or the global pool is for. Segmentation needs it back, so the head is replaced: every fully connected layer becomes a 1×1 convolution, which computes the same function at **every position** instead of once. That is the fully-convolutional insight, and it is why any classifier backbone can become a segmenter.

nodes.label: Blurry boundaries
nodes.sub: which is what the skips fix

d.title: What the skip connections actually recover
d.caption: Downsampling destroys **location** while building semantics: by the bottleneck the network knows there is a cell and no longer knows precisely where its edge is. The skips carry the high-resolution early feature maps across, so the decoder has both — semantics from below, boundaries from the side. Remove them and U-Net's masks lose their edges while keeping their classes.

nodes.label: Concatenated, not added
nodes.sub: the decoder chooses how to use them

d.title: Transposed convolution, and the checkerboard it produces
d.caption: It is not a 'deconvolution' — it is a convolution whose stride is applied to the **output**, so each input pixel contributes to several outputs. When the kernel size is not divisible by the stride those contributions overlap unevenly, and the result is a regular checkerboard artefact. Resize-then-convolve avoids it entirely, which is why most modern decoders do that instead.

nodes.label: Checkerboard artefacts
nodes.sub: a regular grid of brighter pixels

d.title: Grad-CAM, in the four operations it actually performs
d.caption: The whole method is a weighted sum of the last convolutional layer's channels, where each channel's weight is how much the class score responds to it on average. Because it uses the **last** conv layer it is semantically meaningful and spatially coarse — that resolution limit is structural, not an implementation detail.

items.label: Forward to the last conv layer
items.desc: keep its feature maps: C channels of H x W

items.label: Backprop the target class score
items.desc: to those maps, not to the input

items.label: Average each channel's gradient
items.desc: one weight per channel: its importance

items.label: ReLU, then upsample
items.desc: keep only positive evidence; resize to the image

d.title: Reading a Grad-CAM on a real photograph
d.caption: The useful reading is comparative, not absolute. A map centred on the object is reassuring; a map centred on the **background** is the shortcut-detection signal of 9.3 in ML — snow behind the husky, a watermark, a pen mark. And a map is per-class: asking what the second-most-likely class attends to is often more informative than the top one.

nodes.label: The map is on the object
The map is on the background

d.title: Why the ReLU is there
d.caption: The weighted sum contains both positive and negative contributions: regions that support the class and regions that **argue against** it. Keeping only the positive part answers 'what made the model say this class', which is the question being asked. Drop the ReLU and the map mixes evidence for and against into one ambiguous picture.

d.title: A convolution from scratch: the forward pass as a loop nest
d.caption: Six nested loops — batch, output channel, output row, output column, input channel, kernel position — and the innermost line is a multiply-accumulate. Writing it once makes the shapes concrete; it is also roughly a thousand times slower than the library, which is the next section's subject.

nodes.label: for each image in the batch

d.title: The backward pass the usual treatment omits
d.caption: A convolution's backward pass is **three** computations, not one, and the third is the one that is usually skipped. The gradient with respect to the input is a convolution with the flipped kernel; the gradient with respect to the weights is a convolution of the input with the output gradient; and the bias gradient is a sum over everything but the channel axis.

nodes.label: Use the other two to update

d.title: Pooling's backward pass routes rather than spreads
d.caption: Max-pooling's backward pass sends the whole gradient to the **one** input that was the maximum and zero to the rest — which means it must have remembered which that was during the forward pass. Average pooling divides the gradient evenly, and so needs to remember nothing. That asymmetry is why max-pool layers hold an index buffer and average-pool layers do not.

nodes.label: Max-pool forward
nodes.sub: takes the largest of the window

d.title: What the framework actually buys over the loop nest
d.caption: Not autograd — you can write that. The gap is in the four rows below, and it is a factor of hundreds to thousands. im2col turns the convolution into one large matrix multiply so it can reach a tuned GEMM kernel; cuDNN then picks among several algorithms per shape; and fusion removes the memory traffic between the convolution, the bias and the activation.

d.title: The CIFAR-10 model, bottom to top
d.caption: Three stages of convolution and a pooled head — the shape of 2.2 made concrete. Note the two numbers that matter: the spatial size falls 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 while channels rise 3 → 32 → 64 → 128, and the classifier at the top is a single linear layer because global pooling has already removed position.

d.title: Where the parameters are, and why that is the right shape
d.caption: The parameter count **rises** with depth here, which is the opposite of VGG. Each stage doubles its channels, so each convolution's weight tensor roughly quadruples — and yet the head is 1,290 parameters rather than VGG's 124 million, because global average pooling replaced the flatten. The model is 98% convolution by parameter count, and that is the post-2015 shape.

d.title: The training loop, and the five lines whose order is fixed
d.caption: This is the loop every PyTorch model is trained by, and the order is not negotiable. `zero_grad` must come before `backward` or gradients accumulate across batches; `step` must come after `backward` or it applies nothing. The `model.train()` and `model.eval()` pair is outside the inner loop and is the line most often forgotten (1.12).

nodes.label: model.train()
nodes.sub: once per epoch, before the batches

d.title: The same model in PyTorch and in Keras
d.caption: The architectures are identical; the difference is where the loop lives. Keras owns it — you declare the model, compile it with a loss and an optimiser, and call `fit`. PyTorch hands it to you, which is more code for the common case and the only workable option when the loop itself is the thing you are changing.

d.title: Making it smaller: three techniques, three different costs
d.caption: Quantisation is almost free and almost always worth doing — int8 is a 4× size reduction for typically under a point of accuracy. Pruning needs **structured** sparsity to actually speed anything up, because unstructured zeros still occupy a dense matrix multiply. Distillation is the only one that changes the architecture rather than the weights.
cells: under a point, usually; minutes of work

cells.text: no speedup: the matrix is still dense

cells: whole channels go: more accuracy lost
a teacher, and a training run

d.title: Latency and throughput pull in opposite directions
d.caption: They are optimised by opposite choices, which is why one number cannot describe a deployment. Batching improves throughput by amortising fixed costs and **worsens** latency, because the first request in a batch waits for the last to arrive — so a service with a p99 target and a service with a cost-per-million target want different configurations of the same model.

d.title: The runtime landscape, and what each is for
d.caption: The choice is usually decided by the deployment target rather than by speed. ONNX Runtime is the portable default; TensorRT is the fastest on NVIDIA and is NVIDIA-only; Core ML and TFLite exist because a phone is the target. `torch.compile` is the one that requires no export step at all, which makes it the cheapest thing to try first.

d.title: The generator never sees a real image
d.caption: This is the fact that makes a GAN unlike anything else in the course. The generator's only signal is the **discriminator's gradient** — it is told 'that looked fake' and nothing more, never shown a target to match. So there is no reconstruction loss, no per-pixel error, and the quality of the generator is entirely bounded by how good a critic the discriminator is.

nodes.label: Its gradient is the only signal

d.title: Training it: two optimisers, alternating
d.caption: Each step updates one network while the other is held fixed, and the detail that matters in code is `detach()`: when training the discriminator on fake images, the generator must not receive that gradient. Forget it and the generator is updated to make the discriminator's job **easier**, which is the opposite of the game.

nodes.label: Fake -> D, not detached; step G
nodes.sub: G learns to fool the current D

d.title: The equilibrium that does not arrive
d.caption: A GAN's loss curves are **not** progress indicators, which is the single most confusing thing about training one. At the theoretical equilibrium the discriminator is at chance and both losses sit flat — so a falling generator loss can mean the discriminator is losing rather than the samples improving. Judgement has to come from samples and from FID, not from the loss.

nodes.label: At equilibrium D is at chance
The loss is not the metric
nodes.sub: unlike everywhere else in this course

d.title: Mode collapse, and why the game permits it
d.caption: The generator's objective is to fool the discriminator, and producing one perfect image forever does exactly that — nothing in the loss rewards **diversity**. So collapse is not a bug in the optimiser, it is a correct solution to the stated problem, and every fix works by changing the problem: letting the critic see a batch, penalising its gradient, or scoring the distribution rather than the sample.

nodes.sub: D sees the batch, not one sample
